note: Payments Canada's Standard 005 (Standards for the Exchange of Financial Data on AFT Files, 2024 edition, read 2026-10-30) gives the routing number a transfer carries as nine digits: a constant zero, the three-digit institution number and the five-digit branch routing (transit) number; the constant zero is left out here. Standard 006 (MICR-encoded items, 2024, amended to 29 March 2024) gives the same institution (three digits) and branch (five digits). Neither fixes the account number: Standard 005 gives it twelve positions, with embedded blanks or dashes allowed and no justification, and Standard 006 leaves its layout to each member. The Royal Bank of Canada, the largest bank, gives its accounts as seven digits (its wire transfer page, read 2026-10-30), so seven is written. No national check digit is stated in either standard; none is modelled.

sources.title: Payments Canada (Canadian Payments Association), Standard 005: Standards for the Exchange of Financial Data on AFT Files (2024)
sources.said: INSTITUTIONAL IDENTIFICATION NUMBER 9 positions - Numeric - Logical Record Type C, D, E, F, I, J. ... (a) = constant zero (b) = institution number (c) = branch routing number ... PAYEE ACCOUNT NUMBER 12 positions - Alphanumeric

sources.title: Payments Canada (Canadian Payments Association), Standard 006: Specifications for MICR-Encoded Payment Items (2024)
sources.said: Reading from right to left, these groups are: institution number (three digits) and branch number (five digits).

sources.title: Royal Bank of Canada, Wire Transfer
sources.said: Your transit (5 digits, including all zeros) and account number (7 digits). For example: 01234-1234567
